articles.body:
Donna Ganger, the mother of Renee Good, who was fatally shot by a federal immigration officer in Minneapolis earlier this year, said Tuesday she voted for President Trump and thought that federal immigration officers would “protect” Americans.

Ganger said it is “torture” that “as a mom and as a family, we could not protect” Good, who was killed by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer on Jan. 7 in an incident caught on video that triggered a nationwide discussion on the Trump administration’s immigration efforts.

“But no one can protect against others who are determined to disregard our country’s constitutional rules and values,” Good’s mother added. She spoke during a public forum hosted by Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) and Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.).

“I’m a registered Republican,” Ganger said. “I voted for President Trump under the impression that these agents were here to protect the citizens of the United States, innocents like our family and the others here, against terrorists, certainly not to accuse those of us here of being terrorists and take precious lives.”

After the officer fatally shot Good, a 37-year-old American citizen with one son, multiple Trump administration officials said the woman committed “ domestic terrorism ” by allegedly driving her car toward the ICE officer.

“This was an act of domestic terrorism,” then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem said in January.

Video taken by the officer on his cellphone, though, appears to show Good turning her car away from him before the fatal shots were fired.

The incident, along with the fatal shooting of 37-year-old Alex Pretti by Customs and Border Protection (CBP) agents Raymundo Gutierrez and Jesus Ochoa later that month, sparked backlash to the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in Minneapolis.

Blumenthal said Wednesday that Congress “must hold” ICE and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) “accountable” for deaths involving federal personnel.

“Totally unacceptable that there has been no real investigation into DHS/ICE related deaths & injuries,” Blumenthal wrote on the social platform X .

The Hill has reached out to DHS, ICE and CBP for the latest on the investigations into the killings of Good and Pretti.

articles.title: FBI investigates after ShinyHunters hackers claim theft of agents' personal data
articles.summary: ShinyHunters claims it stole personal data of all FBI agents and anyone who has applied for a job with the bureau, including names and addresses.
articles.body: The FBI said it is investigating a hack of its jobs portal, which took down the website entirely on Tuesday. As of Wednesday morning, the site was still not operational. "The FBI is aware of claims regarding unauthorized activity affecting FBIjobs.gov and is currently investigating," the FBI said in a statement to Fox News. ShinyHunters, a criminal hacking and extortion group, took responsibility for the breach and said it has stolen the information of almost all FBI agents and people who applied to the bureau for a job, Reuters reported. FBI WRAPS UP CYBERCRIME OPERATION TARGETING GLOBAL NETWORKS PREYING ON AMERICANS A screenshot of a data sample shared with Reuters contained agents' names, home addresses, Social Security numbers, their assignments and, in some cases, the names of their family members. ShinyHunters said on its dark-web site it targeted the FBI in response to the bureau's May 2026 public service announcement warning organizations about the group's tactics and reiterating that victims should not pay ransom or extortion demands. "Threat actors often use their real or exaggerated claims of access to sensitive or personal information to prompt payment from victims. Victims may receive an extortion email signed as ShinyHunters," the FBI's PSA said. HACKERS THREATEN TO LEAK DATA FROM 275M USERS AFTER BREACHING MAJOR COLLEGE PLATFORM USED NATIONWIDE ShinyHunters has been linked to several high-profile cyberattacks, including the alleged theft of millions of records from "Grand Theft Auto" developer Rockstar Games and a May breach of the Canvas learning platform that disrupted schools across the United States. Earlier this month, Anthropic said it detected hackers tied to the group attempting to misuse its AI tools. articles.title: Trans activists inject themselves with hormones in viral stunt protesting Trump's DOJ deal with NYU
articles.summary: Video shows transgender activists injecting cross-sex hormones outside NYU Langone Health after the DOJ settlement ended sex change treatments for minors.
articles.body: A video showing transgender activists injecting themselves with cross-sex hormones outside New York University's Langone Health hospital is spreading rapidly online, just days after the hospital reached an agreement with President Donald Trump's Department of Justice (DOJ) to cease providing sex-change treatments to minors. "We're taking our HRT here at the doors of the people who have given up to demystify, normalize, and celebrate our trans bodies in the face of NYU's cowardice," a person holding a bullhorn and reading off a script says in the video, referencing hormone replacement therapy drugs. The people in the video, all wearing masks outside, can be seen filling syringes and injecting themselves, including a person in a wheelchair. JD VANCE CALLS ON DOJ TO PROSECUTE ALLEGED FRAUD IN TEEN TRANSGENDER TREATMENT A crowd of supporters, some holding signs saying "Protect Trans Kids" and "Resist," looked on as the stunt was performed. Other protesters held a hand-made banner reading "No compliance with Trump's bias." The video, which was posted to X by Freedom News TV, drew harsh reactions from shocked online viewers. "This is so obviously a mental illness," said online commentator Matt Van Swol. "You cannot watch this video and conclude anything else." "This is a truly crazed movement that has successfully normalized cultish pseudo-medical practices from the outermost fringe of human extremity as a part of suburban elementary school life across America," said author Wesley Yang. "Surely everyone watching these bizarre spectacles understands this." "I see addicts. Addicted to HRT. Addicted to attention. Addicted to constant validation," said Tanya Tay Posobiec. CLEVELAND CLINIC COMMITS $2M TO DETRANSITION CARE UNDER DOJ SETTLEMENT Last week, the DOJ announced that it came to an agreement with NYU Langone and the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center (UPMC) after investigating the institutions for potentially illegally carrying-out on children "sex-rejecting procedures," which proponents often describe as "gender affirming care." "Under the agreements, NYU and UPMC will cease providing these dangerous interventions to minors, which include administering puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones and performing surgical procedures," a DOJ release said. NYU Langone also agreed to pay $8.5 million as part of the settlement, while UPMC agreed to pay $950,000. The DOJ made it clear that the resolution does not confer liability on either of the hospitals, and maintains that the hospitals deny any wrongdoing. "Today’s resolutions send a clear message: hospitals that target children in these practices and then fraudulently obtain payment for the procedures will be held to account."

articles.title: China ‘throwing gasoline on the fire’ in AI data centers race, say lawmakers
articles.summary: Jason Smith and John Moolenaar allege the Chinese Communist Party is exploiting tax-exempt nonprofits while 'waging an influence campaign' against American AI
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: As President Donald Trump prepares to meet with Chinese leader Xi Jinping about the future of artificial intelligence, two top House Republicans are warning that the Chinese Communist Party is "throwing gasoline on the fire" by undermining America's effort to build out AI infrastructure. In a new letter disclosed to Fox News Digital, House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Jason Smith, R-Mo., and House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party Chairman John Moolenaar, R-Mich., asked Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and IRS Chief Executive Officer Frank Bisignano to determine whether money has been funneled from overseas through America’s charitable system to block the data centers needed for the U.S. to compete with China. Specifically, they raised questions about hundreds of millions of dollars that American-born communist tech tycoon Neville Roy Singham pumped into nonprofits and organizations that are now among the leading organizations fighting data center development throughout the country. Recipients of Singham's largesse include the Party for Socialism and Liberation and the ANSWER Coalition, both self-described pro-China communist groups. Earlier this month, activists from both groups carried signs in a Chapel Hill, N.C., protest, merging anti-Trump sentiments with support for communist Cuba and opposition to data centers and AI development, including the message, "SHUT IT DOWN!" "Under no circumstances can we allow an adversary, and our most serious competitor in AI infrastructure, to weaponize our own tax code and harm an emerging American industry," the lawmakers wrote in the letter, sent on Tuesday. FROM AUSTIN TO NEW YORK, PRO-CHINA NETWORK FUELS WEEK OF ANTI-US PROTESTS AS XI MEETS TRUMP The lawmakers allege that influence operations linked to China are exploiting tax-exempt organizations, nonprofit networks and social media campaigns to fuel opposition to the data centers needed to power America’s AI industry. The lawmakers urged the agencies to investigate whether tax-exempt organizations connected to the network have operated for the "private or political benefit of foreign-aligned interests" and whether donor-advised funds and intermediary entities were used to "launder the origin of foreign-directed money into American advocacy." A Fox News Digital investigation found that Singham funneled $285 million since 2017 to six U.S. nonprofits, including his wife Jodie Evan's group, CodePink, through two shell corporations and a donor-advised philanthropy fund run by Goldman Sachs, which said it closed the Singham account in 2024. The nonprofits have functioned with tax-deductible status while actively involved in promoting communist regimes such as China, coordinating street protests and fomenting anti-American rage. They have denied being part of any foreign influence operation, and Singham hasn't responded to requests for comment. Smith said China is helping fuel opposition to American artificial intelligence infrastructure by giving a base to Singham as he funds U.S. nonprofit groups involved in anti-data-center protests. "This is the Chinese helping throw the gasoline on the fire," Smith told Fox News Digital. "The American people need to know that this is not just an organic movement." Smith said Americans have legitimate concerns about data centers, including their effect on electricity costs and water usage. But he said foreign-backed organizations shouldn't be allowed to exploit those concerns to slow U.S. technological development. Smith said that "the Chinese want to stall and slow down the advancement of AI in the United States because they want to win the AI war." "Tax exempt is a privilege. It is not a right," Smith said. "We need to make sure that we’re not subsidizing tax dollars to help create hostility and unrest in our country." Smith also called for greater transparency regarding the flow of money among organizations connected to Singham. He added that the broader issue extends beyond the tax code and could include questions about compliance with the Foreign Agents Registration Act violations. "Transparency is the biggest thing," he said. PROBE INTO 'SUBVERSIVE' ANTI-AI SINGHAM NETWORK IS 'ENORMOUS,' FORMER TREASURY ADVISOR SAYS Moolenaar said organizations presenting themselves as grassroots opposition groups are actually advancing the Chinese Communist Party’s agenda in the U.S. "Groups that portray themselves as grassroots are really more astroturf — very fake — being funded by entities that are working in partnership with the Chinese Communist Party," Moolenaar told Fox News Digital. "The concern is that they are manipulating the messaging and opposition to different American investments, whether it’s data centers or other technological advances, trying to turn the American people against these technologies so that China would be able to have dominance in this area," he said. Moolenaar pointed to the use of grassroots organizations, community groups, propaganda and online bots. "We don’t want foreign entities of concern — countries that may be opposed to American interests — using our system against the American people and trying to manipulate them," Moolenaar said. He said the lawmakers are seeking greater transparency into the organizations’ funding and tax-exempt status, including whether their political activity violates federal rules. "When you see them actively speaking out against American interests and realize that groups like CodePink are aggressively funded by this network, that raises serious concerns," Moolenaar said. The chairman said China’s influence efforts exploit the openness of American society. "The Chinese Communist Party always has the goal of dividing Americans, manipulating and getting their propaganda out," he said. "They don’t have the freedoms that we enjoy, and they try to exploit our freedoms and use that against us." China remains both a major trading partner and a strategic competitor, Moolenaar said, but the United States must avoid becoming dependent on Beijing. "They are a serious adversary," he said. "They are a trading partner, which is true, and we need to have a relationship with them," Moolenaar said. "But at the same time, we do not want to be manipulated, we do not want to become more dependent, and we certainly do not want to be under their thumb." POWER COUPLE OF CHAOS: HOW A TYCOON AND ACTIVIST BUILT A ‘REVOLUTIONARY BASE’ AT THE HOUSE OF SINGHAM The lawmakers noted that a bicameral group of congressional committees, including the Ways and Means Committee, the House Select Committee on the CCP and the Senate Intelligence Committee, has been examining how influence operations linked to the CCP allegedly exploit America’s tax-exempt sector to "sow discord and undermine our democracy." "The CCP consistently identifies political issues under public debate in our country and seeks to corrupt those debates," Smith and Moolenaar wrote in their letter. The CCP, they added, seeks to "heighten divisions between Americans and to degrade our civic processes." The lawmakers specifically pointed to opposition campaigns targeting the construction of data centers, which are critical to the nation’s AI infrastructure. A June report from OpenAI identified two clusters of ChatGPT accounts likely originating in China that were used in covert influence operations targeting U.S. debates over AI and technology policy. One campaign, dubbed "Data Center Bandwagon," generated social media comments and images claiming that data-center construction was raising electricity prices for average families. OpenAI said it found no evidence that the operation achieved meaningful breakout beyond its own activity, but said it demonstrated how foreign operators can exploit existing local concerns to amplify distrust. CHINESE BOT FARM CAUGHT RED-HANDED TRYING TO INFLUENCE HEATED AI DATA CENTER DEBATE The lawmakers also cited a report from the Bitcoin Policy Institute that identified 21 campaigns against data centers led by the Party for Socialism and Liberation across 14 states. The report said those campaigns contributed to 10 data-center moratoria, a permanent data-center ban and four rejected or scrapped projects, representing nearly $23.68 billion in proposed investment. The Party for Socialism and LIberation and the ANSWER Coalition are supported by the Singham network, and a Fox News Digital investigation has traced links between prominent activism against data centers by the Party for Socialism and Liberation, the ANSWER Coalition and other organizations in the Singham network, including BreakThrough News, the People’s Forum, Tricontinental: Institute for Social Research and CodePink. "Our tax code should not be used as a shield for foreign money waging a disinformation war on American AI infrastructure," Smith and Moolenaar wrote. "This is yet another shocking and dangerous example of how malign foreign actors are funneling dollars into the United States to further CCP interests." LAWMAKERS SAY THEY ARE STANDING AT THE GATES AGAINST 'TROJAN HORSES' PROMOTING MALIGN FOREIGN INTERESTS The lawmakers asked Treasury and the IRS to determine whether tax-exempt organizations supporting the network have violated the requirements of their status. Their request includes examining whether organizations operating under Section 501(c)(3) have acted for the "private or political benefit of foreign-aligned interests," rather than for genuine charitable purposes. They also asked whether donor-advised funds and intermediary entities were used to "launder the origin of foreign-directed money into American advocacy." The letter follows earlier oversight by the Ways and Means Committee and the House Select Committee on the CCP into the tax-exempt sector and organizations allegedly connected to Singham’s network. The lawmakers emphasized that opposition to data centers is a legitimate subject for public debate but said Americans should know whether foreign adversaries are attempting to influence those debates through nonprofit organizations, social media campaigns or covert funding channels. "The American people deserve to know which actors adversarial to the United States are trying to undermine these decision-making processes," they wrote. articles.title: Four years ago, we warned about our democracy. Here’s what gives us hope now.
articles.summary: National security experts and over 6,000 Americans have signed the Principles for Trusted Elections to promote democratic stability and bridge political divides through shared values like honest processes and nonviolent campaigns.
articles.body:
Four years ago, we joined other national security leaders in warning that Americans could not afford to take our democratic institutions for granted. Our careers in military, intelligence and diplomatic service have shown us what can happen when citizens lose faith in their elections, when political violence becomes acceptable, and when power begins to matter more than principle.

Four years later, we still believe those risks are real.

But we are writing again for another reason: We have also seen what Americans are willing to do about them. Across the country, citizens are demonstrating in ways big and small that our system of self-government still belongs to “We the People.” We see it in the parent who brings a child along to vote, the military veteran who serves as a poll worker and the candidate who accepts an election result with grace.

In 2022, we believed that instinct deserved a voice, not just an example. We asked Americans to say so publicly through the Principles for Trusted Elections .

Today, more than 6,000 Americans have publicly affirmed those principles, including more than 300 national-security experts and more than 100 organizations, backed by institutions from very different political traditions, including The Carter Center and the Gerald R. Ford Presidential Foundation.

They come from different walks of life, political traditions and points of view. What unites them is a belief that certain principles, about what makes elections trustworthy, how we treat one another and what it means to abide by the same rules, should remain bigger than our political differences.

At a time when it can be easier to retreat to our respective corners, thousands of Americans have chosen instead to publicly affirm that common ground.

The five Principles for Trusted Elections are simple: honest process, nonviolent campaigns, secure voting, responsible oversight, and trusted outcomes. They do not tell anyone which candidate or political party to support. They do not prescribe a particular election law or settle disagreement about how elections should be administered. They establish something more fundamental: the common ground on which those disagreements can occur.

That matters more than it might seem. Research from More in Common, a nonpartisan group that studies political division, found that roughly eight in 10 Americans in both parties say it’s important to respect people they disagree with, yet each side guesses that fewer than four in 10 of the other party feels the same way. The same gap shows up around political violence: researchers have found that Americans on both sides badly overestimate how many of their political opponents would support it, and that simply correcting that misperception measurably reduces people’s own support for violence.

We are far more united than we believe ourselves to be. The assumption that the other side has already given up on the rules, is the real threat.

Everyone who affirms the Principles for Trusted Elections is helping close that gap. That is exactly why your voice matters. Your fellow Americans need to know that you still believe in these rules too.

Start by adding your name at Principles for Trusted Elections, the same way more than 6,000 Americans already have. Then put it into practice: learn how elections actually run where you live, tell the people in your life why these principles matter to you, and ask someone whose politics differ from your own whether they believe in these same principles. You may find you’re not nearly as far apart as you thought. That is the work in front of all of us now, not just those of us who wrote this piece, but every American willing to do their part. Four years ago, we warned that our institutions, our sacred process of self-government, could not be taken for granted. We still believe that. But we have also learned this: it can endure extraordinary pressure, as long as enough citizens decide it is worth protecting.

We added our voices four years ago. Thousands of Americans have added theirs since. We are asking you to now add yours.

Gen. Michael Hayden (U.S. Air Force, retired) is chairman of Team Democracy and former director of the Central Intelligence Agency, director of the National Security Agency and principal deputy director of National Intelligence. Gen. Stanley McChrystal (U.S. Army, retired) served as commander of Joint Special Operations Command. Lt. Gen. Mark Hertling, (U.S. Army, retired) served as the commanding general of the U.S. Army Europe and the Seventh Army. Lt. Gen. Douglas Lute (U.S. Army, retired) served as the U.S. ambassador to NATO and deputy national security adviser.

articles.title: Stanford admits breaking own policy after race-, gender-swapped student photos emerge
articles.summary: Stanford University admitted AI was used to alter a dining hall photo, replacing Billy Ramirez with a Black woman amid Trump administration scrutiny.
articles.body: Stanford University was caught red-handed using artificial intelligence to alter an image promoting its residential and dining offerings, replacing a Hispanic male student with a Black woman. The Stanford Review posted the original dining-hall photo — which shows an Asian woman, a White man and a Hispanic student — alongside the altered version on X. "We have reviewed the matter and confirmed that AI was used to alter the image in violation of university policy. Stanford's AI policy is clear: The use of AI in producing or altering images of Stanford people, events, research, facilities, or achievements is strictly prohibited," a spokesperson for Stanford University said in a email to Fox News Digital. "Both the alteration and lack of disclosure in this case violate that policy. We are working with Residential and Dining Enterprises to provide additional training and ensure proper review of all materials," the spokesperson continued. KEY TRUMP AGENCY PUTS TOP UNIVERSITIES IN CROSSHAIRS OVER ALLEGED RACE-BASED DORM PROGRAMS Billy Ramirez, who was removed from the photo, told the Stanford Review that he was "baffled" when he saw that he was cut out of the photo. "At first, I found it hilarious that they had used AI to completely change our appearances, including my race and gender," Ramirez told the Stanford Review. "But after looking at the comparison, I was also upset because I don’t agree with Stanford making those choices about how we were represented," Ramirez continued. "Seeing my identity changed and being left out of the picture made me feel, in a way, silenced and erased from a representation that was supposed to include me." "Our reporting highlights the need for universities to abandon not just the practice of DEI but the hyper-fixation on the appearance of diversity," the Stanford Review told Fox News Digital. In addition to removing Ramirez from the photo, the appearances of the two students were also altered, making the Asian woman and White man’s faces thinner. FLORIDA STATE UNIVERSITY HIT WITH FEDERAL CIVIL RIGHTS INVESTIGATION OVER RACE, SEX-BASED SCHOLARSHIP PROGRAMS The controversy comes as Stanford faces scrutiny from the Trump administration over alleged race-based discrimination in both its admissions policies and a teacher-certification support program. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER In April, the Trump administration opened a civil-rights investigation into Stanford over allegations that a teacher-certification program reserved full financial support for educators who identified as people of color. The Education Department said it is examining whether the program violated Title VI by conditioning access to benefits on race. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP And in March 2025, the Justice Department launched an investigation into Stanford along with several other universities over whether it was using diversity, equity and inclusion in admission decisions. The outcome of the Stanford admissions review has not been publicly announced.

articles.title: Melania Trump Says Donald Trump ‘Sometimes Doesn’t Want to Hear It’ When She Tells Him What She Really Thinks
articles.summary: “I always say the truth,” the first lady said during an appearance on ‘Fox & Friends’ on Wednesday, Sept. 23
articles.body:
Melania Trump insisted that she tells her husband, Donald Trump, how she really feels about his speeches and interviews, even though he "sometimes doesn't want to hear it"

"I always say the truth," she said during an appearance on Fox & Friends on Wednesday, Sept. 23

The first lady made the comments while discussing what she thought about Trump's United Nations General Assembly speech in New York City the day prior

Melania Trump said her husband, President Donald Trump , "doesn't always want to hear it" when she shares her thoughts.

Speaking on Fox & Friends on Wednesday, Sept. 23, Melania, 56, praised Trump's speech at the United Nations General Assembly in New York City the day prior when questioned whether he'd asked for any feedback from his wife.

"I told him he had [a] great delivery, he did very well. And a great speech," the first lady — who was on the show to discuss the launch of Imperia, a network for women CEOs, and her Fostering the Future Together initiative — said.

She added of her husband, "So I tell him the truth. Sometimes he doesn't want to hear it, what I tell him, but that's okay. I always say the truth."

Elsewhere in the interview, Melania also spoke about how Trump, 80, had been handling his second term as president, in comparison to his first term in office, saying, "He's very focused. He has a lot on his plate. It's very different, what's going on around the world now. But I think he's doing the best that he can."

"He works nonstop. He has the most energy than anybody. He's from morning [until] evening nonstop working," she added.

Trump has previously mentioned Melania giving him feedback, including when he said she wasn't a fan of his onstage dancing earlier this year.

Meanwhile, Melania recently ended a 32-day absence from public view with a speech from the White House Rose Garden on Aug. 20, highlighting her Fostering the Future initiative and plans to expand its national network, PEOPLE previously reported.

At the time, Melania approached the podium and immediately began her speech , saying, "Good afternoon. I heard you missed me?" The audience laughed before she added, "Here I am."

Never miss a story — sign up for PEOPLE's free daily newsletter to stay up-to-date on the best of what PEOPLE has to offer, from celebrity news to compelling human interest stories.

Her comments about Trump on Fox & Friends on Wednesday morning came after the president addressed world leaders across the globe on Tuesday, Sept. 22.

During his speech, he boasted about his record as a peacemaker, as well as questioning whether he should "annihilate" Iran .

The president also took a moment to address CNN during a press exchange at the event after spotting one of the network's reporters days after he announced a ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters from the White House.

"I'm surprised that CNN is here covering me. You shouldn't be here! You should not be here covering me. You said you weren't going to cover me. You shouldn't be covering me," he told CNN reporter Kaitlan Collins.

Collins could be heard replying, "The United Nations allowed us in, sir." She repeated her assertion in a post on X , saying that CNN was "credentialed by the United Nations to cover the General Assembly."

During her exchange with the president, she asked, "Two thirds of Americans don't think the U.S. is winning the war with Iran. When will it end?"

Trump replied, "We're making a lot of progress. Our country is doing really, really well. Thank you very much, everybody."

articles.title: GOP cracks widen over Iran war as vulnerable candidates break with Trump, demand its end
articles.summary: Vulnerable Republicans Ashley Hinson, Mike Rogers and Jon Husted break with Trump on the Iran war as gas prices reshape toss-up Senate races.
articles.body: Vulnerable Republicans running for their political lives have, for months, kept quiet or sided with President Donald Trump on the war in Iran. But as costs rise and voters pepper them with questions on the campaign trail about when the fighting will end, some are changing their tune and breaking with Trump, arguing the war must end to lower prices — including lawmakers who previously voted to continue the conflict in the Middle East. Rep. Ashley Hinson, R-Iowa, former Rep. Mike Rogers, R-Mich., and Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, are all running in toss-up races that will define the balance of power in the Senate. TRUMP-BACKED IOWA US SENATE HOPEFUL SAYS IRAN WAR MUST 'BE BROUGHT TO A SUCCESSFUL AND IMMEDIATE END' Hinson, whose agriculture-heavy state is getting hit with high diesel costs, argued that lawmakers needed to suspend the gas tax, pause diesel exports, "unleash E-15 everywhere we can," reinstate biodiesel tax credits and create a diesel relief program. "These actions to lower costs are needed ASAP, and the war needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end," Hinson said. Her race against Iowa state Rep. Josh Turek is listed as a toss-up, according to the Cook Political Report. Hinson, however, has voted against every war powers resolution offered in the House. Notably, she voted against the successful war powers resolution when seven House Republicans, including two other Republican members of the Iowa House delegation, voted for it. FOX NEWS POLL: 71% THINK TRUMP ADMINISTRATION LACKS PLAN TO END IRAN WAR Rogers has been out of Congress since 2015 but is running in one of the most-watched toss-up races this cycle against Abdul El-Sayed, and Republicans hope to flip a state that eluded them when Trump ran for his second term two years ago. Shortly after Hinson’s shift in position, he released an ad echoing an immediate end to the war. But weeks earlier, the former lawmaker, who voted in favor of the war in Iraq in 2002, told Fox News Digital at the GOP’s made-for-TV huddle in Dallas that he wanted to see the war come to an end. "Well, first of all, I'd like to see this thing come to an end. They need to find a way to get this thing ended," Rogers said. "I think that's certainly where Michigan voters, Michigan families are." 7 REPUBLICANS REBEL AGAINST TRUMP, VOTE WITH DEMS TO REIN IN IRAN WAR POWERS "Again, I think we have to understand, do we want Iran to have a nuclear weapon? I think most people overwhelmingly say no," he continued. "Would they like this to come to an end? I say absolutely yes." Husted, who is running in another toss-up contest against former Sen. Sherrod Brown in Ohio, has also pivoted. And like Hinson, he has voted against every war powers resolution that has hit the floor in the Senate. "The war needs to come to an end as quickly as possible so that we can lower gas prices," Husted told Politico. Husted, like others, has pushed several times for a "brief and successful" end to the war over the last seven months, and like several Republicans, has made the case that getting the Strait of Hormuz running and open was a paramount goal. Olivia Tripodi, a spokesperson for Husted, told Fox News Digital that the lawmaker's "position has not changed. Any accusation otherwise has not listened to Sen. Husted over the last seven months." "Since the beginning of the conflict in Iran, he has called for the military operation to be successful but brief so that gas prices can go down for Ohioans, but that enacting a War Powers Resolution would undermine the U.S. negotiating position and potentially put American troops and allies at risk," Tripodi said. "He has also supported the president’s efforts to negotiate a settlement to end the war, despite the Iranian side’s refusal to negotiate in good faith and its efforts to extend the conflict and bomb U.S. ships." Some Republican leaders are encouraging candidates to break with Trump to make their own bespoke campaigns, particularly as the war’s unpopularity continues to increase. And so, I encourage most candidates to run their own campaigns." "I mean, obviously, the president's gonna be a factor in every election. It’s a midterm election, he's not on the ballot," Thune said. And I think that's the best way to do it."

articles.title: FIRST ON FOX: Rubio ramps up birth tourism crackdown hours before Xi touches down in US
articles.summary: Marco Rubio announced visa restrictions on those who engage in or facilitate birth tourism as Xi Jinping arrives for a high-stakes state visit.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX — Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced Wednesday that the Trump administration is moving to restrict visas to individuals who "engage in or facilitate" birth tourism hours before Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in the United States for a state visit, Fox News Digital has learned. "By restricting visa issuance of those who both engage in and profit from this fraud, we are sending a clear message: The United States will not allow foreigners to exploit our immigration system and violate the sanctity of U.S. citizenship," a statement from Rubio obtained by Fox News Digital states. The restrictions target foreigners who "knowingly engage in, have engaged in, or facilitate birth tourism," including non-citizens who work in the birth tourism industry, so-called fixers who coach visa applicants to commit fraud, as well as others "who support, abet, and enable commercial birth tourism." BIRTH TOURISM FIGHT SHIFTS TO US ‘TROPICAL MATERNITY WARD’ WITH HISTORY OF CHINESE EXPLOITATION Birth tourism is the practice of traveling to the United States for the primary purpose of giving birth so the child obtains U.S. citizenship. China has been a particular focus of federal efforts to combat the practice, with Justice Department cases targeting large-scale birth tourism operations catering predominantly to Chinese clients. Chinese nationals have traveled to clinics on the West Coast and to Saipan — part of the U.S. Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands — to give birth. Rep. Brandon Gill, R-Texas, who chairs a House Oversight task force investigating birth tourism, has also singled out China and Russia in raising concerns about the practice. China could also stand to gain from a reduction in birth tourism as the country faces a steep demographic decline. Young people leaving for the United States, a process made much easier if they’re already citizens, could exacerbate China's troubles on that front. TRUMP’S TOUGHER ROUND-TWO BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP STRATEGY HINGES ON KEY LEGAL DISTINCTION, EXPERTS SAY Cracking down on birth tourism has been a cornerstone of the Trump administration’s immigration agenda. Alongside countering birth tourism, the Trump administration has also unsuccessfully sought to overturn birthright citizenship as part of its push to address what it feels are abuses of the American system. After the Supreme Court struck down the federal government's initial attempt to do away with birthright citizenship, President Donald Trump issued two follow-up executive orders. One sought to deny citizenship to children born to members of designated terrorist organizations and the other directed the State Department to deny travel visas to or pursue removal actions against individuals believed to be in the country for the purposes of birth tourism. AMERICA AND CHINA ARE FIGHTING FOR THE FUTURE OF AI — CHIPS ARE THE BATTLEFIELD "The Trump Administration is using every tool at our disposal to defend the integrity of U.S. citizenship, protect American public benefits and U.S. taxpayers from exploitation, and safeguard our national security," Rubio said in his statement. articles.title: SHOCK POLL: Powerful blue state gov's lead shrinks to single digits weeks before election
articles.summary: Bruce Blakeman trails Kathy Hochul by just nine points in a new Siena poll, closing the gap in a state where Democrats outnumber Republicans two-to-one.
articles.body: Democrats outnumber Republicans by a roughly two-to-one margin in blue-leaning New York State, but a new poll indicates Republican gubernatorial nominee Bruce Blakeman has cut his deficit to Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul to single digits with just six weeks to go until Election Day. Hochul, who is running for a second full four-year term steering the nation's fourth most populous state, stands at 50% support among likely voters in New York, with Blakeman at 41%, according to a Siena College poll conducted Sept. 11-17 and released on Wednesday. Blakeman, the Nassau County executive on New York's Long Island, trailed Hochul by 10 points in Siena's August survey. The one-point movement by Blakeman, who is aiming to become the first Republican in nearly a quarter-century to win an election for governor in New York, is within the survey's margin of error. "With six weeks until election day, voters offer good news to both Hochul and Blakeman. She now has the support of 50% of voters and saw her favorability and job approval ratings edge into positive territory. He now trails by single digits – well, nine points – in a state where Democrats outnumber Republicans by more than two-to-one," Siena pollster Steven Greenberg said. CHECK OUT THE LATEST FOX NEWS POLLING IN THE MIDTERM ELECTIONS Greenberg noted that at this point four years ago, Hochul held a 17-point lead over then-Rep. Lee Zeldin, the GOP nominee. But Zeldin closed the gap and ended up losing to Hochul by only six points in the 2022 election. "Currently, Blakeman is doing a better job with Republicans, leading 88-8%, than Hochul is with Democrats, leading 81-11%," Greenberg added. The GOP nominee is also edging Hochul 44%-39% among independent voters. "All polls continue to show Kathy Hochul's downward spiral and me closing the gap as New Yorkers learn more about my plan to cut income taxes by historic margins and slash electric bills in half," Blakeman argued in a statement after the release of the Siena poll. But the new poll indicates that two-thirds of New York State voters, including 37% of Republicans, think Hochul will win re-election. DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB Blakeman is a strong supporter of President Donald Trump, who in February endorsed his bid for governor. But Trump's support may be doing Blakeman no favors, with half of likely voters, including a quarter of Republicans, saying it's a negative for the GOP nominee's campaign. Hochul was endorsed earlier this year by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, the first socialist mayor of the nation's most populous city, reciprocating her backing during his own historic mayoral run last year. By a 50%-30% margin, voters said Mamdani's support for Hochul is a plus for the governor's bid for re-election. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Then-Lt. Gov. Hochul was sworn in as New York’s first female governor in August 2021 after Gov. Andrew Cuomo, in the middle of his third term, resigned amid multiple scandals. Hochul has seen her political standing rise over the past year and a half as she's increased her resistance to Trump's unprecedented second-term agenda. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Asked about the poll, Hochul campaign spokesperson Ryan Radulovacki, referring to Blakeman, told Fox News Digital, "No one wants a Trump puppet in the governor’s mansion who will cut their healthcare, raise their costs, and let ICE trample their rights." "They trust Governor Hochul’s record of investing in public safety, lowering crime, and putting money back in their pockets – and they know she’ll fight for their families, not Trump," he added. The poll, which was conducted by telephone and text-to-web collection, surveyed 1,144 likely voters in New York, with an overall margin of error of plus or minus 3.9 percentage points for core questions.

articles.title: Trump to ask Xi to free wrongfully detained US citizen as wife speaks out
articles.summary: President Trump plans to ask Chinese President Xi Jinping to release Dr. Youlin Chen, a U.S. citizen charged with espionage after two years in China.
articles.body: President Donald Trump plans to ask Chinese President Xi Jinping to release wrongfully detained U.S. citizen Dr. Youlin Chen, the man's family told Fox News after his wife and the wife of another detainee spoke exclusively to "Fox & Friends" Wednesday. The wives of two wrongfully detained Americans in China made a plea for Trump to intervene in their husbands' detention during an interview with Fox News senior foreign correspondent Gillian Turner. Yugang Rong and Sylvia Zin implored Trump to intervene in the cases of their husbands, Chen, a seismic and nuclear researcher, and Min Zin, a scholar with a focus on Myanmar, respectively. The pair are the only two U.S. citizens in China that have been designated by the U.S. State Department as wrongfully detained. CHINA’S XI SET TO ARRIVE IN WASHINGTON FOR HIGH-STAKES TRUMP SUMMIT AS AI SUPREMACY BATTLE LOOMS LARGE "My husband is an American citizen. He is the father of my son and we terribly miss him," Rong told Turner. Chen was taken from outside the Beijing airport by Chinese agents in November 2024, according to a website dedicated to his release. After Chinese agents took him, they reportedly seized his cellphone, iPad, laptop and cameras and repeatedly logged onto his email accounts and accessed his devices. His wife believes he was taken because of his seismic research into nuclear activity. "It's his research work. He has been doing a lot of research on how to monitor nuclear tests," she told "Fox & Friends." His research, according to the website, "focuses on the Earth's crustal structures in Asia using regional earthquake data, including data sourced from and in collaboration with earthquake scientists in China." In one of his publicly available reports he used geophysical research methods to detect North Korean nuclear tests. China charged Chen with espionage, but he has yet to receive a trial despite over two years of imprisonment. He has not been allowed any contact with his family. DAUGHTER OF DETAINED CHINESE PASTOR SAYS SHE HAS 'HOPE' AFTER LEARNING TRUMP MAY RAISE CASE WITH XI JINPING Sylvia Zin, meanwhile, does not understand why her husband, whose research focuses on military government and Chinese-Myanmar relations, was taken. "Unlike Dr. Chen, I really have no idea why, what in his research that they would be interested in. He is an open source researcher, and all of his work is published on their website," Zin told Turner. MY FATHER IS A PASTOR, IMPRISONED IN CHINA. PRESIDENT TRUMP, PLEASE SAVE HIM Both women made a plea to the president to intervene. "At this point, I think the president is the only person who can move ahead in this case and bring him home," Zin said. PASTOR FREED FROM CHINESE PRISON AFTER TRUMP RAISED HIS CASE WITH XI JINPING Both Zin and Rong said they were hopeful that Trump would bring their husbands home. "President Trump has done a lot for us. He has personally been involved in this case. I know whenever he [gets] personally involved in cases, Americans come home," Rong said. US MARINE VETERAN RELEASED FROM RUSSIAN PRISON AFTER 1,666 DAYS OF DETENTION The Trump administration has succeeded in securing the freedom of 83 U.S. nationals detained abroad in the past year, according to a report from the James W. Foley Legacy Foundation. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News' Gillian Turner contributed to this report.

articles.title: Supreme Court to hear Missouri redistricting case for third time
articles.summary: Justice Brett Kavanaugh accepted an emergency appeal in the Missouri redistricting case as the 2025 map faces its third Supreme Court review.
articles.body: The U.S. Supreme Court will hear arguments in a Missouri redistricting case for a third time after Justice Brett Kavanaugh accepted a request to intervene in the case once again Tuesday night. The divisive redistricting map drawn in 2025 would grant Republicans an additional seat in the House of Representatives if it is put in place ahead of the 2026 elections. A federal judge in Missouri ruled in favor of the 2025 map last month, but the Supreme Court put a stay on that ruling just two weeks ago. Opponents of the map issued an emergency appeal to the Supreme Court late Tuesday night after the St. Louis-based Eighth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled in favor of the new map on Monday. FEDERAL APPEALS COURT ORDERS MISSOURI TO USE CONGRESSIONAL MAP REJECTED TWICE BY SUPREME COURT Kavanaugh handles emergency requests for the state of Missouri and directed supporters of the new map to respond to the appeal by Wednesday at 2 p.m. ET. The development is the latest in a roller-coaster ride of legal decisions that have seen the new map fly up and down between federal and state courts, the Supreme Court and the Missouri Supreme Court. ELECTION CHAOS IN THIS RED STATE JUST GOT EVEN STRANGER FOR REPUBLICANS AFTER SUPREME COURT RULING The case began when Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins rejected a petition for the 2025 map to be placed on the ballot for a vote in 2026. Instead, the new map was used to determine congressional districts for the state's primary elections. The Democratic group behind the petition, People Not Politicians, asked a state court to intervene, saying the group's petition of 300,000 signatures should have triggered a referendum on the new map under Missouri's constitution. The Missouri Supreme Court agreed, writing that the 2025 map cannot go into effect "unless and until approved by the voters at the November 2026 general election." MISSOURI HIGH COURT BLOCKS GOP-BACKED CONGRESSIONAL MAPS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS; TRUMP BLASTS 'RIDICULOUS' RULING Hoskins then appealed the case to the Supreme Court, but Kavanaugh declined to hear his request on Sept. 4. Meanwhile, Republican candidates who won primary elections based on the 2025 maps brought up a separate case in federal court, arguing that if the general election takes place under the 2022 map their districts would be very different from the primary maps. Many general election voters, they noted, would also be presented with options they had no role in voting for during the primaries. SUPREME COURT AGAIN BLOCKS MISSOURI FROM USING TRUMP-BACKED CONGRESSIONAL MAPS Eighth Circuit Judge Stephen R. Clark ruled in favor of those candidates and issued an order requiring that the 2025 maps be used in this year's elections, effectively contradicting the state Supreme Court. This time, People Not Politicians asked the U.S. Supreme Court to intervene, and Kavanaugh agreed. The court issued an unsigned order blocking Clark's order until the Eighth Circuit issued a formal ruling in the case. The Eighth Circuit then fast-tracked the case and ruled in favor of the 2025 map. MISSOURI SUPREME COURT THREATENS SECRETARY OF STATE WITH CONTEMPT AMID INTENSIFYING REDISTRICTING BATTLE People Not Politicians filed their latest request for an intervention on Tuesday night, arguing that the court's ruling against the new map was still in effect, and pointing to statements from Missouri election officials saying it is too late to change what maps are used in the upcoming elections. The Missouri Association of County Clerks and Election Authorities already announced it will not be using the 2025 map for November, arguing in an appeal filing that the state does not have enough time to provide new ballots. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Ballots have been printed, and Missourians have already voted. Thousands more will vote before this order seeks to take effect. Officials should stop wasting taxpayers’ money on pointless legal action and instead focus on administering our elections," People Not Politicians director Richard von Glahn said in a statement. The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: The top moments from Iran president’s tense visit to US soil as war rages
articles.summary: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian cast Iran as a victim of U.S. aggression at the United Nations General Assembly as a delegate walked out.
articles.body: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian defended Tehran’s conduct in its war with the United States on Wednesday, taking aim at President Donald Trump and vowing that Iran would not surrender during a fiery address before world leaders at the United Nations General Assembly. The speech follows months of fighting, failed diplomatic efforts and mounting international pressure on Tehran, giving Pezeshkian a high-profile platform to defend Iran’s actions and challenge the U.S. account of the conflict. "America and Israel attacked us, equipped with the latest technology and weapons systems, and our people stood steadfast. Yes, they did hit us, but we did not bend the knee. We did not bow our head," said Pezeshkian. "Those who are terrorists and train and protect terrorists describe us as such. We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists." Fox News Digital compiled the top moments from Pezeshkian’s speech and the developments unfolding both inside and outside the U.N. ONE GLARING ISSUE GOES UNADDRESSED IN UN CHIEF'S HIGH-STAKES TALKS WITH IRAN'S PRESIDENT Protesters gather outside UN, jeering the Iranian president's visit Pezeshkian’s fiery attacks on Trump and the United States came amid a hostile reception in New York City, where protesters gathered to denounce the Iranian government as its president addressed world leaders at the United Nations. Former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani joined a "Free Iran" rally outside the U.N., where protesters denounced Tehran as Pezeshkian addressed world leaders. Demonstrators waved Iranian flags while denouncing Iran’s government over its repression of political dissent, restrictions on women’s rights and treatment of opposition figures. US delegate walks out as Iran vows 'we will not bend the knee' at UN As the emcee announced Pezeshkian's impending speech, audible boos erupted from the protest crowd outside the UN as the leader walked out onto the stage. A member of the U.S. delegation walked out of the General Assembly hall after Pezeshkian began criticizing the United States during his speech, Fox News Digital previously reported. Fox News Digital reached out to the U.S. Mission for comment. TRUMP DEFENDS US INTERVENTIONS ABROAD AHEAD OF 'BIG DECISION' ON IRAN: 'SETTLING YEARS OF UNFINISHED BUSINESS' America on trial, Trump dubbed a 'bully' Pezeshkian used his speech to defend Iran’s conduct during the war and take aim at the United States and Israel. "The United States using weapons with multiple warheads targeted that sports hall. … They martyred, assassinated our scientists, our men, women and children," he said. "This is what the United States seeks to do with all countries — [to] sacrifice the population of a country in order to achieve [its] goals," Pezeshkian added. CENTCOM has denied that U.S. forces carried out the strike on the sports hall in Lamerd, saying American forces did not strike the city or anywhere within 30 miles of it on the opening day of Operation Epic Fury. FIVE TOP TAKEAWAYS FROM TRUMP'S HIGH-STAKES UN SPEECH TO THE WORLD Pezeshkian said that the U.S. and Israel have learned that Iran cannot be made to surrender, reiterating that Iran is "not afraid of fighting" and would defend the country "until our last breath." TRUMP WARNS IRAN WILL BE HIT 'REALLY HARD' IF NUCLEAR NEGOTIATIONS COLLAPSE AGAIN During a moment of his speech, Pezeshkian held up props showing photos of the late Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and Iranian schoolchildren killed during the beginning of the conflict. "Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country. And we defended ourselves with utmost strength. America and Israel attacked us," Pezeshkian said. He also used the opportunity to take shots at Trump, accusing him of "bullying" Iran. "More must be understood by Mr. Trump and those who seek to bully us, that we are ready for dialog and diplomacy and negotiations without accepting the language of force," Pezeshkian said. Trump addressed leaders Tuesday and said he faced a "big decision" between reaching a deal with Iran or, in his words, "annihilat[ing] the Islamic Republic," before U.S. officials later met with Iranian officials. "Going back to the words of the president of the United States yesterday … everything uttered about our country was against the very essence and charter in the spirit of the United Nations," Pezeshkian said. "He must know that the resistance of the Iranian people will increase in the face of sanctions, and increased bullying, because all of us under law will never bow our head or bend at the knee." Administration officials quickly pushed back on Pezeshkian’s attacks and disputed his account of the conflict. "I think sponsoring terrorist organizations in the region to attack your neighbors, attack energy infrastructure, attack civilian sites is a violation of the UN system. So I don't know what's standing. Iran has to lecture anyone on human rights or the international system. When they habitually violate it," said Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Rubio added that Iran has no credibility defending the international order because its regime has repeatedly violated it. "The President is courageously ensuring that such an evil country never possesses a nuclear weapon, which will make the entire world safer and more stable," she added.

articles.body:
Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) shifted the Florida governor’s race to a toss-up amid a rough electoral environment for Republicans as they head into the midterms.

In a post on the social platform X Wednesday, DDHQ said that the race had gone from “Leans Republican” to “Toss Up.” DDHQ stated that Rep. Byron Donalds (Fla.), the Republican nominee in the race, currently has a 60 percent chance of winning, an 8-point drop from earlier this month.

Donalds’s challenger, Democrat David Jolly, currently has a 40 percent chance of taking the election.

The apparent tightening of the race for Florida’s top job in a state that President Trump has won in the last three elections may be a warning sign for Republicans as the midterms approach.

Republicans are facing the unpopularity of the war in Iran, Trump’s sagging approval numbers and polling favoring Democrats as they attempt to keep control of Congress.

Donalds removed some mentions of Trump’s name in a newer layout for his website Tuesday. The old layout featured a banner at the top of Donalds’s webpage that read, “Chip in to Support Trump Endorsed Byron Donalds,” and text below it that said, “TRUMP-ENDORSED.”

If users were to go down on the page, there was another bar that noted the endorsement next to a photo of Trump.

Donalds’s newer layout only showed Trump’s endorsement in a box next to other endorsements for the Florida representative. A Donalds campaign source told The Hill that Trump remained “all over the website” and that the president’s support “is worth its weight in gold, and we are grateful to have it.”

Other Republican candidates facing tight races , Rep. Ashley Hinson (Iowa), who is running for Senate, and former Rep. Mike Rogers (Mich.), making an upper chamber bid in the Wolverine State, recently distanced themselves from the president on the subject of the Iran war, with both noting its effect on the cost of living.

articles.title: Judge skeptical of White House press ban on Politico, MS NOW, CNN: Due process ‘wasn’t followed’
articles.summary: President Trump’s decision to ban a trio of news outlets from the White House complex last week and revoke their hard press badges appeared to be on thin ice Wednesday after a key hearing where the sides presented their arguments. Due process “wasn’t followed here,” U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, said near the…
articles.body:
President Trump’s decision to ban a trio of news outlets from the White House complex last week and revoke their hard press badges appeared to be on thin ice Wednesday after a key hearing where the sides presented their arguments.

Due process “wasn’t followed here,” U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, said near the start of the afternoon hearing.

CNN, Politico and MS NOW sued on First Amendment grounds after they were denied access to the White House grounds on Saturday. The five major television networks that comprise the rotating pool covering Trump’s daily activities have since pulled out in solidarity with the banned outlets.

Wednesday’s hearing came as each of the major networks weighed how to cover Trump’s expected return to Washington from New York, where he traveled to meet with world leaders at the United Nations General Assembly.

The president is slated to greet Chinese leader Xi Jinping on Wednesday evening, an event that typically would garner a large amount of media attention and drive the news cycle for hours.

“These are urgent matters,” Theodore Boutrous, an attorney for the media outlets, told the judge. “We’re at war. World leaders are coming to Washington.”

Boutrous urged Kelly on Wednesday to immediately restore the three outlets’ credentials, arguing that Trump’s ban amounted to “viewpoint discrimination” that violates the First Amendment. He also said the decision came “completely out of the blue.”

The Department of Justice (DOJ) contends the president has a right to decide who gains “privileged access” to certain spaces, pointing in court filings to a 2025 appeals court decision that allowed the administration to temporarily bar The Associated Press from the Oval Office and Air Force One.

“Access to the White House is a privilege, not a right,” DOJ attorney Michael Velchik said, later adding that “at the very least, the president may exclude anyone he wants from the Oval Office.”

He cited national security concerns as the rationale for the current restrictions, an argument that Trump has used repeatedly to justify his more controversial initiatives, from sweeping global tariffs to the construction of the White House ballroom .

But that is a different argument from what Trump used to justify the ban on the three media organizations. The president initially said the ban was based on cumulative negative coverage by each of the outlets.

“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States,” Trump wrote Friday on Truth Social .

Boutrous said of the president: “He wears his heart on his sleeve.”

Letters sent to each outlet this week identified a handful of stories the White House said “threatened national security and/or spread falsehoods,” including coverage of the Iran war, the Republican midterm convention, Russian sanctions and other military matters.

“Your organization has exhibited behavior in violation of the standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including by trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information,” each letter stated.

Boutrous called the cited articles “garden-variety reporting,” arguing that Trump’s use of national security as a “magic word” doesn’t hold up.

The White House Press Office has set a deadline of Friday at 5 p.m. EDT for the outlets to contest the allegations, a postdeprivation process Velchik argued is sufficient.

But Kelly wasn’t convinced, signaling that the letters may have come too late.

“I don’t know [that] a letter they got after the pass was revoked could provide them with the kind of standards that they’d have to conform their conduct to,” the judge said.

The due process argument played heavily in a 2018 decision in which Kelly found that former CNN White House correspondent Jim Acosta’s constitutional rights were likely violated when his hard press pass was revoked under the first Trump administration.

It involves a 1977 ruling from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit in which the court held that the White House could not arbitrarily deny a press access to a journalist without procedural due process.

“I was as surprised as anyone when I dug in to look at the law that in Sherrill back in the ’70s, that the D.C. Circuit held there was a due process interest in the White House hard pass for the media,” Kelly said during Wednesday’s hearing.

DOJ lawyers want that 50-year-old precedent overturned, something that could be done only by a higher court.

The Trump administration walked into court expecting a loss. Across a series of Truth Social posts and public comments, Trump referred to Kelly as “totally disloyal” and said the judge would “probably” rule against him.

But the president deflected on Tuesday when asked whether he would restore access for CNN, Politico and MS NOW if ordered to.

“I think we have a right to clean out fake news,” Trump responded to a question from Reuters during a bilateral meeting at the U.N. General Assembly.

Trump’s ban was widely panned by First Amendment groups and has sparked a rare moment of solidarity among the press corps, including conservative media outlets with an audience that is more supportive of the president.

A number of major media companies filed an amicus brief with the court in support of CNN, MS NOW and Politico, writing the ban “injures the public interest, and that unassailable First Amendment law makes any viewpoint-based decision to bar reporters from a nonpublic forum constitutionally repugnant.”

Kelly did not issue a ruling from the bench Wednesday, saying he would have one “as soon as I can.”

In the Acosta case, the judge’s decision came two days after the hearing.

articles.title: Kaine calls Iran war ‘triply illegal,’ says it should ‘end immediately’
articles.summary: Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.) called on the Trump administration Wednesday to swiftly end its military operations against Iran amid legislative pressure to bring this monthslong conflict to a close. Kaine noted the House’s passage of three Iran war powers resolutions, calling the conflict “triply illegal” in comments to reporters on Capitol Hill shared by CSPAN. …
articles.body:
Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.) called on the Trump administration Wednesday to swiftly end its military operations against Iran amid legislative pressure to bring this monthslong conflict to a close.

Kaine noted the House’s passage of three Iran war powers resolutions, calling the conflict “triply illegal” in comments to reporters on Capitol Hill shared by CSPAN .

The lawmaker said the Senate, which passed a war powers resolution he introduced in June, is “likely to pass a second one soon.” Four Republican senators crossed party lines to support the first measure.

However, Kaine acknowledged the resistance of the Trump administration to public pressure to end U.S. military operations against Iran.

“The war should end immediately because it’s illegal and foolish,” Kaine said, adding, “I don’t think you can expect the president to do that.”

Critics of the conflict have cited the U.S. service members who have died during the Iran war and rising global energy rates tied to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a major oil trading corridor located in the region.

The war has also become increasingly unpopular in polling of the American public, with three quarters of respondents in a July Marquette Law School Supreme Court survey saying the conflict was “not worth the cost.”

Gas prices in the U.S. have surged amid the Iran war, with the national average of standard gas sitting around $4.47 per gallon on Wednesday, up from an average of about $3.17 per gallon a year ago, according to AAA .

Last week, the president said at a political rally in North Carolina that rising gas prices were “a very inexpensive price to pay for what we’ve done.”

Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio), who is engaged in a tightly contested reelection race this November, told Politico on Tuesday he would like to see the war “come to an end as quickly as possible so we can lower gas prices.”

A spokesperson told the outlet the senator does not plan to support Democrats’ war powers resolution. This measure does not carry the force of law.

GOP Sen. John Kennedy (La.) told CBS News’s Nikole Killion on Wednesday that “we all want the war to end” but also withheld support for a war powers resolution.

“I don’t support Congress pulling the rug out [from] under our commander in chief and just forcing him to stop immediately prosecuting the war, particularly when we’re winning,” Kennedy said. “I don’t support that, and I think the genesis of most, not all of that, but the genesis of most of that is political, and I think it would hurt America.”

articles.title: Collins rips report on pay-for-play allegations: ‘Partisan hit job’
articles.summary: Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) ripped a recent report about an FBI inquiry into an alleged pay-to-play scheme as a “partisan hit job” and “offensive.” “I do not understand how anyone would take the word of a felon who’s been convicted twice — twice — two separate cases of five counts of money laundering, counts of…
articles.body:
Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) ripped a recent report about an FBI inquiry into an alleged pay-to-play scheme as a “partisan hit job” and “offensive.”

“I do not understand how anyone would take the word of a felon who’s been convicted twice — twice — two separate cases of five counts of money laundering, counts of bank fraud, false submissions to the [Federal Election Commission],” Collins told The Wall Street Journal in an interview that aired Wednesday, referencing former Navatek CEO Martin Cao.

“He is a convicted liar, and when you contrast that to my decades of honest public service … with the utmost integrity … it is so offensive,” she added, calling the report “a partisan hit job.”

ProPublica released a bombshell report on Tuesday , reporting that the FBI investigated an alleged scheme between the senator’s office, Collins’s super PAC and defense contractor Navatek.

The reporting cites testimony from Kao in addition to 2019 emails and correspondences seen by the outlet showing that Collins’s super PAC asked Navatek executives for donations in exchange for the senator working to award Navatek more government contracts. Collins is the chair of the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee.

Many of the bribery allegations came from Kao, who pled guilty for several campaign finance violations in 2022. Kao was separately sentenced to 87 months in prison in 2025 regarding COVID-19 relief wire and bank fraud.

ProPublica also reported that many of the federal officials investigating the case around the alleged Collins pay-to-play scheme were removed from the Trump administration or quit during the president’s second term.

The allegations raise serious questions for Collins, who is running against Democrat Troy Jackson in a tough reelection battle. Several members of the Collins campaign have strongly denied the allegations raised in the report.

“What they’re saying is that those of us who have worked for Senator Collins — long-time campaigns, federal work as well — the allegation is that I, we, all of us, for $40,000 in risking serious federal jail time for a contribution to the campaign, would engage in bribery, extortion, and pay for play, and I find that incredibly offensive,” Collins campaign manager Steve Abbott told reporters on Wednesday.

He called the allegations “false” while noting that the FBI informant was coming from “a guy who was awaiting sentencing for a significant federal offense, who was trying to get his sentence reduced, as the article states correctly.”

Collins deputy chief of staff Annie Clark also aggressively denied the news outlet’s reporting in a lengthy statement on the social media platform X .

“There have never been any allegations of wrongdoing by the Collins for Senator campaign, and the campaign was never the target of the FBI investigation,” Clark said Tuesday, while calling Kao an unreliable and dishonest witness.

“It is important to note that during the Biden Administration the FBI and the Department of Justice thoroughly investigated the Navatek matter,” she wrote. “The Collins campaign cooperated fully with the FBI throughout the investigation, producing all of the documents it requested and serving as fact witnesses in official settings.”

articles.title: Trump pushes to admit 17,500 White Afrikaners from South Africa in 2027 refugee cap
articles.summary: The Trump administration on Wednesday proposed raising the refugee cap for the coming year to 17,500 people, which is a historically low figure, and which President Trump argued should primarily be given to white Afrikaners. The move raises by 10,000 last year’s refugee cap – the lowest proposed rate in the history of the program…
articles.body:
The Trump administration on Wednesday proposed raising the refugee cap for the coming year to 17,500 people, which is a historically low figure, and which President Trump argued should primarily be given to white Afrikaners.

The move raises by 10,000 last year’s refugee cap – the lowest proposed rate in the history of the program – while retaining the unusual mandate to resettle one ethnic group from South Africa.

Started in the aftermath of World War II, the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program (USRAP) has offered refuge to those around the globe fleeing persecution and danger. Before last year, the program has never been used to offer assistance to one ethnic minority.

In asserting Afrikaners deserve the protections, the State Department repeated a number of claims that have been denied by the government of South Africa.

“Afrikaners face the seizure of agricultural property without compensation; government policies designed to dismantle equal opportunity in employment, education, and business; and hateful rhetoric fueling disproportionate violence against racially disfavored minorities,” the department stated in a letter to Congress obtained by The Hill.

“The United States anticipates that Afrikaners from South Africa will fully assimilate into the United States in a manner that preserves taxpayer resources for U.S. citizens and does not anticipate other countries resettling Afrikaners.”

The government of South Africa has repeatedly denied Trump’s claims surrounding Afrikaners, calling them “completely false.”

“This reality is further corroborated by the actions of individuals who, despite having availed themselves of this preferential immigration program, have since resolved to return home,” spokesman Chrispin Phiri told The Associated Press in May when Trump raised the refugee cap to 10,000 from the original 7,500.

Refugee resettlement agencies have condemned the focus on one group

“A refugee program that centers one group and sidelines all others is an abdication of our global humanitarian leadership and an abandonment of thousands of vulnerable families who put their faith in our country,” Krish O’Mara Vignarajah, president and CEO of Global Refuge, said in a statement.

“Behind that closed door stands everyone this country once promised to protect: the Afghan interpreter, the persecuted pastor, the mother fleeing a war zone who once had reason to believe America would keep its promise.”

HIAS, formerly known as the Hebrew Immigrant Aid Society, noted in a press release that there are more than 200,000 refugees in the pipeline, something they argued was “leaving refugees in true need of protection stranded in precarious situations around the world.”

The U.S. has thus far failed to meet the updated cap imposed by Trump. CNN reported in July that the administration had accepted 7,700 Afrikaner refugees but came across unusual snags in the process, including having to reject applicants due to criminal backgrounds and also having potential refugees seek to delay their departure to wrap up business in South Africa.

The outlet reported that denial rates based on a criminal past were in the low tweens, while typically such rejections are in the single digits.

Under the Biden administration, the State Department recommended a cap of 125,000 refugees.

articles.title: ICE officer who shot Austin man wasn’t wearing body camera: Reports
articles.summary: The Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer who shot a Venezuelan man in Austin while he was in his vehicle this weekend was not wearing a body camera during the incident, according to multiple reports. The officer fired at Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, while he was making a DoorDash delivery, according to his attorney,…
articles.body:
The Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer who shot a Venezuelan man in Austin while he was in his vehicle this weekend was not wearing a body camera during the incident, according to multiple reports.

The officer fired at Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, while he was making a DoorDash delivery, according to his attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch. He was taken to the hospital before being released into ICE custody.

The ICE agent was reportedly not wearing a body camera, NBC News reported Tuesday, as the Travis County District Attorney’s Office continues its investigation into the shooting. Lincoln-Goldfinch also alleged ICE agents “sideswiped” Garcés Pérez’s vehicle before the incident.

The local district attorney’s office sent letters to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and ICE, requesting Garcés Pérez remain in the country “as a material witness in the ongoing investigation” about the shooting. The Venezuelan man, who his attorney says was legally seeking asylum in the U.S., was ordered for deportation.

Lincoln-Goldfinch wrote on social media that Garcés Pérez “remains gravely ill, with the bullet still lodged in his body, and he remains in ICE detention.”

“According to the detainee who spoke with his wife, Wilber appeared discolored, extremely swollen, and in significant pain,” she continued, before demanding that he be transferred back to a hospital for appropriate medical care.

When asked about the shooting, ICE denied Lincoln-Goldfinch’s reports that it refused to remove the bullets from Garcés Pérez’s body, denied pain medication or forced him to sleep on the floor.

“Contrary to their claims, this person is an illegal alien who has no legal status to be here and has been given some of the best medical care he’s ever received in his life,” DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement sent to The Hill.

When The Hill asked for comment on the allegations surrounding the officer’s body camera, an ICE spokesperson deferred to a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) “CORRECT THE RECORD” press release on the incident. The statement denies Lincoln-Goldfinch’s claims surrounding Garcés Pérez detention conditions and immigration status but does not address reports about the agent.

Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) wrote in a Wednesday post to social platform X that he plans to visit South Texas Detention Complex, where Garcés Pérez is being held.

“He needs a doctor, not deportation. I’ll report back on what I find,” Casar added.

More than half of the agency’s field officers have already been outfitted with the body camera, according to The Associated Press . The others were expected to receive them by the end of September.

A February 2025 ICE directive states its officers should activate these cameras at the beginning of enforcement activities — including arrests, stops and searches.

The agency’s policy, however, would reportedly only release footage if the administration determined doing so would be “in the best interests of the agency,” even in cases of bodily injury or death while in custody, the AP first reported in August.

articles.body:
Republican Sens. Bernie Moreno (Ohio) and Jim Banks (Ind.) warned of a situation similar to previous investigations into President Trump’s ties with Russia amid a GOP push to question Donald Trump Jr. over reporting that a Russian oligarch funded his after-wedding party.

“I couldn’t care less who throws a private citizen a wedding after-party,” Moreno said in a Tuesday post on the social platform X.

“Subpoenas of presidential family members must pass a high bar. We can’t let the Senate become a partisan tool used to harass private citizens in pursuit of political points. Republicans must learn the lessons of the past, we can’t fall prey to Russiagate 2.0,” he added.

A day later, Banks responded to Moreno’s X post with his own, saying that “the last Russia hoax cost this country years of progress.”

“We are not doing it again over a private citizen’s wedding,” he added. “Don Jr. is a businessman, not an administration official. There is no evidence he sold access to the presidency.”

Multiple Republican senators have lent their support to Sen. John Curtis’s (R-Utah) push for the Senate Judiciary Committee to investigate the president’s son due to his business dealings and gifts he received from a Russian businessman linked to the Kremlin.

In a letter to leaders of the committee, Curtis noted Trump Jr.’s “lavish wedding afterparty” on a “private island” that Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev spent money on, per recent reporting from ProPublica.

During Trump’s first term, former special counsel Robert Muller’s investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election and possible collusion between the Trump campaign and Moscow implicated six ex-Trump associates. However, it did not outright accuse the president of committing a crime and did not find evidence for collusion.
