articles.title: Newsmax CEO says he asked Trump to ‘reconsider’ White House media outlet bans
articles.summary: Newsmax CEO Chris Ruddy on Tuesday said he asked President Trump to reconsider his ban on CNN, Politico and MS NOW reporters from covering his administration and the White House. “I’ve urged the president to reconsider his position,” Ruddy told “BBC Newsnight” in an interview. “I hope he will. I think it would be a…
articles.body:
Newsmax CEO Chris Ruddy on Tuesday said he asked President Trump to reconsider his ban on CNN, Politico and MS NOW reporters from covering his administration and the White House.

“I’ve urged the president to reconsider his position,” Ruddy told “BBC Newsnight” in an interview. “I hope he will. I think it would be a smart decision going forward. As much as he may be justified by what he feels is very biased reporting, I think we should always err on the side of the constitutional freedoms.”

Ruddy said he thinks Trump is “right [in] that they’re not necessarily honest and fair.”

“Well, the Constitution doesn’t protect fair and honest reporting,” he added. “It only protects the free press and being a press owner or certainly only a public company or being the head of a public company here that’s a media company.”

Ruddy made similar remarks to The New York Times , saying the ban “would set a bad precedent for all media, including conservative outlets like Newsmax.”

“Newsmax asked tough questions during both the Obama and Biden administrations, and at no point did anyone suggest that we might be banned,” Ruddy told the Times.

On Wednesday, a federal judge in Washington, D.C., appeared skeptical of Trump’s ban on the reporters. U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, said in response to the outlets’ lawsuit against the administration that due process “wasn’t followed here.”

Trump issued his ban on reporters from the three outlets last Friday, accusing them of “fake news,” with reporters losing their passes while on White House grounds the next day. All three outlets sued the administration on Monday, arguing it is violating the First Amendment and harming their ability to share information about the government with the public.

Attorneys for all three outlets jointly argued that the ban “could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles.”

Trump defended the ban as not being “an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish.”

“It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America,” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Monday. It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!”

The Department of Justice said it stands by the president’s ban and called access to the White House complex a “privilege.” The department argued that the administration saw what it described as failures to meet basic standards of “professionalism and decorum” and to protect “sensitive or classified information” from being published by the press.

Other news outlets condemned the ban, including contributors at Fox News. Major TV networks on Monday pulled from the White House pool covering Trump for wider media distribution in solidarity with their CNN, Politico and MS NOW peers.

articles.body:
Lawsuit challenges ‘medically frail’ exemption

What does it mean to be “medically frail?” A new lawsuit is challenging how the Trump administration plans to exempt medically frail people from Medicaid work requirements.

Medicaid enrollees, alongside several major health care advocacy organizations and the city of Columbus, Ohio, said the administration’s final rule implementing work requirements is not what Congress intended.

They argue the rule narrowly defines who qualifies for the law’s medical frailty exclusion, putting people with serious physical and mental health conditions at risk of losing Medicaid because of new reporting and verification requirements, even though Congress categorically excluded medically frail people from the requirements.

The coalition is asking a federal court in Maryland to vacate the rule, alleging it’s “arbitrary and capricious and contrary to law.” The suit also alleges violations of the Administrative Procedure Act, the law governing how regulations are issued.

The work requirements are set to take effect in January . Beneficiaries who are part of the Medicaid expansion population must work or volunteer at least 80 hours per month, attend school at least part time or participate in job training.

Expansion states are responsible for ensuring working-age recipients are meeting the requirement unless they are disabled, caring for young children or have a serious health condition.

The rule implicitly links the definition of medical frailty to a person’s ability to work. To qualify for an exemption, a person must demonstrate that their condition prevented them from meeting the work requirement.

The lawsuit is the latest attempt to challenge the work requirements. In June, about two dozen states sued the Trump administration over the “medically frail” definition. A federal judge in July denied the states’ request to block the rule while the lawsuit is agued.

Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage (R), who is running for Congress, said Monday his son’s father-in-law is being deported, calling the situation “not right.”

LePage, running to succeed outgoing Democratic Rep. Jared Golden (Maine) in the state’s 2nd Congressional District, told reporters his relative is being deported because “he came from a country that’s not to the liking of certain people” in Washington, D.C.

“That’s not right. He has a work permit. He should be allowed to stay,” LePage said, according to video shown on WGME-TV in Portland, Maine.

Maine has been among many states subject to President Trump’s immigration crackdown, with WGME-TV reporting last month that federal immigration officers had made 482 arrests in the state so far this year, citing data from the Deportation Data Project.

In July, a federal immigration officer fatally shot Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Biddeford, Maine. Guerrero, a 25-year-old man from Colombia, was not the target of the warrant Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers were executing when he was shot, Sen. Angus King (I-Maine) told The Associated Press at the time.

ICE said at the time the man was attempting to flee the scene, and did not say whether he was the target of the operation. Guerrero’s death sparked backlash in Maine and from Democratic lawmakers against the widespread deployment of federal immigration authorities.

Relatives of David Brouillette, the ICE officer who fatally shot Guerrero, have also warned that the man has a history of violent behavior and mental health issues.

LePage said Monday he “probably” would not go after migrants who have “been here for decades” and have work permits. Instead, the GOP congressional candidate said the federal government should target those in “gangs” and with criminal records.

LePage, who preceded Maine Gov. Janet Mills (D) in the governor’s mansion, is running against state auditor Matthew Dunlap (D) in November. As of Wednesday, Decision Desk HQ gives the former Republican governor a 64 percent chance of winning the general election.

Voters are turning to AI on politics. Is it up to the task?

Artificial intelligence is playing a growing role in how voters get information about politics and elections, raising fresh questions about how the technology could influence the way voters stay informed.

From chatbots to standard internet searches , voters this election cycle are interacting with AI-generated content, even when they may not realize it.

Recent research on voters’ use of AI is forcing campaigns to rethink their digital strategies and reminding election officials the importance of upkeep regarding information online.

“While people may have and should continue to have … a healthy dose of skepticism about some of the outputs, the reality is that [AI] outputs are going to be playing an increasing role,” Max Read, the director of civic innovation at the research organization Institute for Strategic Dialogue, told The Hill.

“Both as a primary information source and point of information gathering for voters, but also impacting the information environment in more subtle ways,” Read said.

A handful of researchers this year are exploring how often voters intentionally use AI to answer election-related questions or accidentally interact with AI-generated content on social media or search engines.

While some say it is likely too early to determine the extent of which AI is reshaping the information ecosystem, many researchers agree it is playing a larger role than in past elections.

Amid the billions of questions chatbots receive daily, a study commissioned by the left-leaning marketing firm Orchestra found about 650,000 of these prompts relate to politics.

articles.body:
Former White House communications director Anthony Scaramucci said Wednesday that former Trump White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt would have advised President Trump to not enact his recent press ban.

“A [former Trump White House chief of staff] John Kelly would have told him not to do that. I actually think a Karoline Levitt would have told him not to do that, because it’s going to backfire,” Scaramucci said on The Hill’s “Rising” of the banning of MS NOW, CNN and Politico from the White House.

“It looks like there’s a bubble around the president. They’re more or less letting him do what he wants, or whatever the reactions may be. And there’s nobody pushing back on him and saying, ‘Here are the consequences,’” he added later.

Trump’s decision to bar three news outlets from the White House last week and revoke them of their hard press badges looks to be in danger following a key hearing on Wednesday.

U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, who was appointed by the president, said at the beginning at the hearing that due process “wasn’t followed here.”

CNN, Politico and MS NOW sued on First Amendment grounds in the wake of being denied access to the White House grounds over the weekend. The five major television networks participating in the rotating pool covering the president’s daily activities have since backed out of doing so in solidarity with the three outlets.

Trump has a historically contentious relationship with the press, often accusing them of false reporting.

On Monday, Trump denied he was “instituting an assault” against the press after the three outlets he banned from White House coverage announced plans to sue due to the restriction.

articles.title: Farm state Republicans feel the pressure from rising diesel prices
articles.summary: Farm state Republicans are increasingly pressing the Trump administration and Congress to take action to bring down diesel prices, underscoring how rising costs have become a political liability for the GOP heading into the November midterms. articles.body:
Farm state Republicans are increasingly pressing the Trump administration and Congress to take action to bring down diesel prices, underscoring how rising costs have become a political liability for the GOP heading into the November midterms.

Rep. Ashley Hinson, the Iowa GOP Senate candidate, on Tuesday demanded action, calling for the House to return to session “immediately” to pause diesel exports, suspend the gas tax and create a diesel relief program for farmers and truckers.

Her call comes just a day after she argued that the military conflict in Iran needs to be brought to a “successful and immediate end” and that Iowans are “being squeezed” by higher costs at the pump and grocery store.

She’s hardly alone in raising the alarm. Other Iowa Republicans, including Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Zach Nunn, whose seats are rated as toss ups by the nonpartisan Cook Political Report, and Sen. Chuck Grassley have backed a temporary embargo on diesel exports.

Former Rep. Mike Rogers, the GOP Senate candidate in Michigan, has also supported the proposal, arguing that “American energy should provide relief to American families first.”

National average diesel prices hit an all-time high Monday, reaching $6.51 per gallon. By contrast, diesel cost $3.52 a gallon on average before the United States and Israel launched strikes against Iran.

“Diesel is the fuel most closely tied to inflation because of its use in the supply chain,” GOP analyst Rob Stutzman told The Hill. “The higher diesel prices means higher prices for everything on a store shelf or Amazon delivery.”

Farmers in particular have seen the impact firsthand, as they depend on diesel to operate tractors and other equipment used through the planting and harvesting seasons.

“I think Republicans in farm states are victims of disastrous Trump policies related to tariffs and the Iran War. The promises by Trump about tariffs haven’t come true for most farmers. And Trump has never articulated a strong case for the Iran War and has been promising its imminent conclusion for months. When your party’s leader isn’t leading a parade into a dark alley, you head in a different direction,” Stutzman said.

President Trump called for a ban on diesel exports at a Tuesday press conference in New York.

“I’ve said, ‘Let’s not send out the diesel.’ We make a lot of diesel, and it could have a little bit of an effect on regular automobile gasoline because when you do that, you know it’s a sort of a flow. It’s a balance,” Trump said during a bilateral meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly.

But the White House on Wednesday denied a report from Politico that it is planning a 90-day ban on diesel exports. The White House referred The Hill to Energy Secretary Chris Wright’s comments to The Wall Street Journal, in which the secretary said that the administration would not halt all diesel exports and would instead take a voluntary approach to bringing prices down.

Farm state Republicans, meanwhile, have been in a tough spot, as they campaign on the message of affordability that is increasingly at odds with the state of the economy at home.

For some, the diesel issue carries added political stakes as they run in competitive seats. A recent Marist poll found Hinson trailing Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek by eight points, underscoring the pressure on Republicans to address voters’ concerns about the cost of living as they head into the final stretch of the campaign.

“I think it behooves Republicans that represent, particularly these districts, right, the farm states, to speak up on that stuff, and to be vocal about it, so I appreciate what’s happening in Iowa because like this idea that we’re willing to sacrifice whatever, you know, for this cause, and again, it’s not just Iran. You know, the president is saying no one wants a nuclear Iran, and we’re willing to pay a little more for that…but it has dragged on. The mission has been convoluted, and it’s been unclear and opaque,” GOP strategist Amy Koch said.

“And this strategy has been botched, in my opinion. And so, seeing that and knowing that, and knowing that six months later it continues with apparently no end in sight, except maybe after the election, that’s hard for voting Iowans or voting Minnesotans to just go, ‘Oh, okay, I’m just supposed to hang in here longer,”’ she added.

A GOP political operative in Georgia, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, told The Hill that there’s a lot of pressure in his state “to remove the state sales tax on gasoline and diesel.”

Even if Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) calls on the House to come back to address the diesel issue, as Hinson has called for, Koch said she thinks very little progress will be made.

“You’d have to have some kind of a big global agreement for the House, the Senate, and the president to actually get something done,” Koch said.

Johnson canceled the last two weeks of the September session, arguing that much of the legislative action has been stalled in the Senate and that members could use the extra time to campaign in their districts. The lower chamber is expected to return to session on Nov. 9, after the midterm elections.

articles.body:
Wright throws cold water on diesel export ban

Energy Secretary Chris Wright threw cold water at the idea of a full ban on diesel exports Wednesday.

“The blunt tool of banning diesel exports definitely doesn’t work,” Wright was quoted as saying by the news outlet Reuters .

“If you can’t export the diesel that comes out of our refineries, you run out of places to store it, and you have to reduce US refining, which would put upward pressure on gasoline prices and jet fuel prices,” he said.

The Wall Street Journal reported that at its event, Wright said that the administration would not halt all diesel exports and would instead take a voluntary approach to bringing prices down.

Shortly after those remarks, Politico reported that the White House was gearing up for a 90-day ban on diesel exports. The White House denied the report and referred The Hill to Wright’s remarks in the Journal.

The comments come one day after President Trump expressed support for a diesel exports ban.

“I’ve said, ‘Let’s not send out the diesel.’ We make a lot of diesel,” Trump said. “I’ve called for it within my people. I’ve been talking about it.”
